The final carry component estimates **loss within one second, conditional on carrying**. It uses a physics-informed competing-risk likelihood with a shared survival probability, logistic arrival gates, and an additive tackle rate. It is separate from end-of-possession xLoss. **own derivation**

## Cohort and evaluation

The cohort contains **9,114 carry attempts, 456 losses (5.003%), across ten SkillCorner matches**. Goalkeeper carriers, shot-ending individual possessions and successful tails shorter than one second are excluded. Goalkeepers remain among defenders. Individual-possession start and end must be matched. Loss-ending possessions additionally require an associated matched on-ball engagement (OBE). This removes 20 unverified loss parents: 34 sections, including 20 terminal losses and 14 preceding successful sections. OBE is not required for successful-ending possessions and is never a predictor. SkillCorner possession loss concerns individual control, including some out-of-play cases where the team retains the restart; it does not always mean a team turnover. Only the final failed section is a loss; early and zero-duration failures retain the one-second Bernoulli target. Failed passes are outside this task. This training cohort differs from the additional snapshots available for arbitrary-frame evaluation. **design choice**

Five outer folds hold out two complete matches each. Spline transformations and smoothing selection use training matches and inner validation matches; metrics concatenate the five held-out prediction sets, with each observation appearing once. Metrics, including quantile bins, are recomputed on that union; neither fold ECE nor fitted parameters are averaged. The null model uses each outer training set's loss frequency. Gain is `1 − CE_model / CE_null`; ECE uses ten equal-count quantile bins weighted by their observation counts. Physical-model CE uses natural logarithms and a probability floor of 1e-6. The CatBoost protocol uses standard float64 log-loss clipping; the downloadable common-floor sensitivity separates numerical tail effects. No resampling or post-hoc calibration is used in the final model. These ten matches also informed model-family development: this is a development benchmark, without an untouched external evaluation. **design choice**

## Log-linear proportional-hazard-inspired model and splines

The starting model uses $\lambda(t)=\lambda_0\exp(\beta_v v_B+\beta_B B(t))$. The additive version replaces the linear covariate shapes with penalized splines; it preserves positive multiplicative rates, defender reachability and shared survival. Both are likelihood-based. This comparison examines functional form, not a standalone Cox proportional-hazards test. See the [ball-drive vignette](vignettes/01_ball_drive_risk/01_ball_drive_risk.ipynb) for equations, references and tracking-based kinematic justification.


The following **historical ablation uses the original 9,148 sections / 476 losses**. Its within-cohort comparisons remain useful; its values should not be subtracted from the final filtered-cohort results as an isolated model improvement.

| Model | Cross-entropy | Gain over null | Quantile ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Log-linear baseline**; historical TTI; Euler | **0.158336** | **22.609%** | **0.902%** |
| Additive speed/boundary reference; historical TTI; Euler | 0.156796 | 23.361% | 0.614% |
| Preserve defender initial speed above the cap | 0.156568 | 23.473% | 0.621% |
| Add individual interception-angle spline | 0.155175 | 24.154% | 0.697% |
| Use signed boundary distance | 0.153320 | 25.060% | 0.644% |
| **Historical exponential Euler, refitted** | **0.153312** | **25.064%** | **0.642%** |

The historical exponential-Euler Brier score is **0.041968**, ROC AUC **0.87246**. Mean predicted loss is **5.268%**, versus **5.203%** observed. The angle improves cross-entropy without improving pooled ECE in this comparison. The integration change has negligible predictive effect; exponential Euler is retained for probability-mass preservation. Rows describe successive changes on the same cohort, not isolated causal effects.

Signed boundary distance matters mainly for unusual outside-pitch states: 210 trajectories project outside during the horizon, including 45 already outside at the initial frame. About 80.5% of its cross-entropy improvement comes from those 45 rows. This correction should not be presented as a general improvement on ordinary interior carries. Annotation and synchronization noise remain possible; no labels were changed to obtain these results.

The downloadable [metric table](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/metrics.csv), [calibration bins](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/calibration_deciles.csv) and [source hashes](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/provenance.json) contain aggregate results from the outfield log-linear baseline and audited runs 14–15. The baseline and spline rows use the same 9,148 states, labels and outer match pairs; the final changes are presented separately.

## Final physical model on the verified-loss cohort

The OBE-filtered run refits the same physical specification, preserving natural proportions and the fixed one-second Bernoulli target. Four six-fit/two-validation rotations inside each outer eight-match training set select smoothing; all five select `main_1_angle_100`. Pooled held-out CE is **0.143483**, null CE **0.198722**, gain **27.798%**, and ten-quantile ECE **0.475%**. Brier is **0.040068**, ROC AUC **0.88547**, and loss-class PR AUC **0.30837**. Predicted loss averages **5.059%**, versus **5.003%** observed.

On these same retained rows, the historical weights give CE **0.143921** and ECE **0.633%**. The refit improves CE only modestly; much of the difference from the historical all-row score reflects cohort selection, not a better functional form. No difficult retained example is removed based on model error. [Final physical metrics](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/filtered_physics_metrics.csv), [fold parameters](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/filtered_physics_parameters.csv), [calibration bins](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/filtered_calibration_deciles.csv), [audit provenance](docs/ball-drive-benchmark-provenance.json).

### Final exploratory CatBoost and training-only resampling

This separate experiment uses the **same 9,114 sections and 456 losses** as the final physical model. It does not replace the likelihood in the package. Its 50 inputs are derived from the initial tracking snapshot and projected constant-velocity carrier path:

| Feature block | Count | Definition |
|---|---:|---|
| Carrier speed | 1 | Initial speed magnitude from the current centred seven-frame tracking estimate |
| Boundary distance | 3 | Signed minimum distance to any of the four lines at 0, 0.5 and 1 s |
| Defender TTI | 9 | Three smallest TTI, independently ranked at 0, 0.5 and 1 s |
| Encounter curve | 11 | All-defender encounter probability at 0, 0.1, …, 1 s |
| Carrier and goal geometry | 8 | Initial/projected x/y, distance and bearing to opponent goal centre |
| Three nearest defenders | 15 | Initial distance, defender speed, relative closing speed, transverse relative speed and front/back position cosine for each fixed defender identity |
| Local geometry | 3 | Defender counts within 2/5 m and position-angle cosine between the nearest two |

For $r=x_D-x_B$, $n=r/\|r\|$ and $w=v_D-v_B$, closing speed is $-n\cdot w$ and transverse speed is $\sqrt{\|w\|^2-(n\cdot w)^2}$. Front/back cosine compares the defender's **relative position** with carrier velocity; it is not the angle between their velocity vectors. It is undefined below carrier speed 1 m/s. CatBoost handles missing values. Future observed position, outcome, engagement, duration, receiver identity and player/team identities are not features.

TTI uses **vmax = 7 m/s**, linear and turning acceleration **7 m/s²**, preserved initial overspeed, fixed-position Pleuler realignment and no reaction delay. Encounter features use $F_i(t)=\operatorname{sigmoid}[\pi(t-\tau_i(t))/(\sqrt3s)]$ and $E(t)=1-\prod_i(1-F_i(t))$, following the reachability interpretation [@bekkers2025; @spearman2018beyond]. Crucially, **s comes from the corresponding physical training fit**, not the former fixed 0.45 s: six-match values inside validation rotations and eight-match values for outer refits, identical in both sampling arms. Inner s spans **0.28076–0.31419 s**; outer s **0.28866–0.30600 s**. The full ten-match export is never used to create held-out benchmark features.

Five outer folds hold out two entire matches. Four inner **6 fit + 2 validation** rotations within the other eight select the full **36-configuration** grid: depth 4/6/8 × learning rate 0.02/0.05/0.1 × L2 1/3/10/30. Each candidate builds 3,000 trees; pooled validation CE selects a common prefix among 25, 50, …, 3,000. There is no early elimination of slower configurations. Native CatBoost binary Logloss, `SymmetricTree`, `Plain` boosting, Bayesian bootstrap (temperature 1), random strength 1 and border count 254 are used, without custom derivatives or class weights. Symmetric trees are the standard native policy; the grid explores capacity, step size and regularization without changing the architecture. The selection principle follows the [CatBoost parameter documentation](https://catboost.ai/docs/en/concepts/parameter-tuning); the particular grid and match grouping are project choices.

For each selected configuration, seeds 19/41/73 produce an average-probability ensemble: four inner fits and one outer eight-match refit per seed. This gives **159 fits per task, 1,590 in total**. Each task is one sampling arm and outer fold. Selected prefixes range from 200 to 1,125 trees; none reaches the cap. Parameters are selected separately within each outer fold, not from its test score. [Selected configurations](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/catboost_final_parameters.csv).

The sampled arm retains every loss and samples nine successes per loss uniformly without replacement, **inside fitting subsets only**. Validation, calibration and test retain natural prevalence. Candidate selection for this arm evaluates prior-corrected probabilities. If successes are retained with probability $q=9N_{loss}/N_{success}$, the known sampling correction is

$$\operatorname{logit}(p_{population})=\operatorname{logit}(p_{sample})+\log q.$$

This is a class-prior correction, not a Bayesian parameter prior. Separately, Platt and isotonic are fitted to natural-label **inner OOF raw ensemble scores** on the eight training matches, then applied to the two test matches. Platt uses fixed weak regularization C=1000; isotonic is standard monotone regression with clipped extrapolation. No prior correction is applied before these learned calibrators, and no calibrator is tuned on test data.

| Training / output | Pooled CE | Gain over null | Quantile ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Natural, raw** | **0.139855** | **29.623%** | **0.490%** |
| Natural, Platt | 0.139934 | 29.583% | 0.483% |
| Natural, isotonic | 0.147136 | 25.959% | 0.468% |
| 10% loss, raw | 0.150333 | 24.350% | 3.311% |
| **10% loss, analytic prior correction** | **0.139928** | **29.586%** | **0.397%** |
| 10% loss, Platt | 0.140049 | 29.525% | 0.401% |
| 10% loss, isotonic | 0.143942 | 27.566% | 0.413% |

Natural raw has the lowest observed CE. Platt substantially repairs raw resampling calibration, but analytic prior correction is marginally better. **Resampling produces no meaningful CE benefit here**, while pooled ECE improves slightly. CatBoost natural reduces CE by **2.53% relative** to the physical model (+1.83 percentage points of gain over the same null), improving eight of ten matches. Its loss PR AUC is **0.30794**, essentially unchanged from the physical **0.30837**. Reporting the best observed output is exploratory; it is not a test-selected deployment rule. [All final metrics](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/catboost_final_metrics.csv).

Isotonic assigns zero loss probability to one actual loss in each arm; natural isotonic also assigns one to a success. Standard float64 log-loss strongly penalizes these rare extreme errors, although ECE remains small. With a **common 1e-6 floor applied to every model**, isotonic CE is 0.142259 (natural) and 0.141504 (sampled), still worse than CatBoost raw/Platt. This sensitivity does not change the prespecified primary scores. [Common-floor diagnostic](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/catboost_common_floor.csv).

The representations overlap substantially with Stalpaert's spatial, pitch-control and path-density information, without replicating his exact feature transformations. Limited data scale is a plausible explanation for the absent resampling benefit, but labels, features, splitting and architecture also differ; these results cannot isolate the cause or prove that useful 2D information is exhausted. Earlier 33-feature and richer-feature results remain in the [historical exploration table](data/benchmarks/ball_drive/catboost_exploration.csv). [Final audit provenance](docs/ball-drive-benchmark-provenance.json).

### Further extension motivated by the published resampling result

The large within-study CatBoost gain motivates a further hybrid: use a cross-fitted physics prediction plus 2D/context features, then compare natural training with 10% loss training at fixed match folds. The tests above did not include the fitted likelihood score as an input. Tree splits can express nonlinear interactions and subgroups absent from the present additive rate. Resampling changes their training emphasis; it does not create information. Evaluate on natural held-out data and fit any calibration inside training/validation only. This hybrid is an extension to test, not an already established gain for PRESS. **design choice**

The present likelihood's sampling experiments showed no convincing held-out gain after accounting for the changed class prior; raw resampling distorted calibration. Published CatBoost + sampling results therefore motivate this combination rather than replacing the TTI with a more agile routine. The sources do not isolate architecture, features and sampling across datasets. **design choice**

## Closed model specification

The carrier is a point moving as $x_B(t)=x_B(0)+v_B(0)t$. The defender routine retains the historical fixed-position turning delay $v\theta/a_{turn}$, followed by straight-line acceleration toward the target. Maximum linear and turning accelerations are separate user parameters; the benchmark sets both to **7 m/s²**, with **vmax = 7 m/s**. Initial speed above vmax is retained without additional acceleration. The engagement-disc experiment is not included. The runtime does not take an observed acceleration input or use future observed acceleration.

At every integration step, the signed boundary margin is the minimum inward distance to the four lines of a centred **105 × 68 m** pitch. It becomes negative outside; the carrier is neither stopped nor assigned an automatic loss. The log tackle rate combines a baseline, additive speed and boundary effects, and a small individual angle spline. The angle is between carrier velocity and the defender's predicted final approach to the projected carrier position. It is a motion-based heading proxy, not observed posture. Its contribution is masked for carrier speed below 1 m/s or undefined direction. **own derivation**

Speed and boundary use five-knot restricted cubic bases; angle uses four knots. There are no interactions between these effects. The selected smoothing setting was `main_1_angle_100` in all five outer fits. Exponential Euler uses dt = 0.04 s and shares remaining survival mass across defenders. It is first-order for time-varying rates; mass preservation does not establish timestep convergence. The final refit estimates all coefficients and basis transformations anew on the ten matches; fold coefficients are not averaged.

## Use the fitted model on a pitch

This executable example uses **synthetic tracking**, with the verified full-data model bundled in the package. The pitch is illustrative; it contributes no benchmark observations.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fitted-drive-pitch
#| fig-cap: "Synthetic frame evaluated by the final fitted model, using the package's pitch visualization."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PRESS import PRESS
from PRESS.datasets import load_demo_match
from PRESS.model import BallDriveModel
from PRESS.visualization.plot import plot_pi

tracking, possessions, actions, _ = load_demo_match()
model = BallDriveModel.pretrained()
press = PRESS(tracking, possessions_data=possessions,
              actions_data=actions, ball_drive_model=model)
frame_id = int(press.get_frames(valid_only=True).frame.iloc[0])
press.compute_ball_drive_loss(frame_id, t_press=1.0)
result = press.get_ball_drive_result(frame_id)
print("Model:", result["params"]["model_id"])
print("One-second carry-loss probability:",
      round(float(result["Ball drive loss probability"]), 4))
plot_pi(press, frame_id)
plt.show()
```

`BallDriveModel.from_json(path)` also loads an exported model. `model.predict(...)` evaluates arrays directly, including shorter horizons. Initialization performs no fit. The fitted path is selected explicitly; omitting `ball_drive_model` retains the legacy log-linear API. Short-horizon outputs are supported by integration, but independent calibration at those horizons has not been established. See the [function reference](api.qmd).

## Final refit and checks

Run 47 fits the accepted specification once on all ten matches and the final 9,114-row OBE-verified cohort. It is **not another test fold** and produces no replacement for the OOF metrics above. Its arrival dispersion is **s = 0.299632** and baseline tackle rate **lambda0 = 0.344563 s⁻¹**; lambda0 is an intercept parameter, not an average tackle probability.

The fit records successful convergence, maximum gradient 0.00378 and a valid Laplace approximation. A separate public-runtime export check verifies prediction parity and probability mass. Loading the exported JSON through the frozen package reproduces all 9,114 training predictions within **3.06 × 10⁻⁸** absolute probability; maximum survival-plus-cause mass error is **2.22 × 10⁻¹⁶**. Short horizons 0, 0.17, 0.4 and 1 s are monotone in the verification sample. [Refit provenance](docs/ball-drive-refit-provenance.json).

## Limits and extensions

The model represents average player skills and individual reachability, with limited encounter geometry. Successful and failed carries overlap substantially in available 2D features; this does not prove that all useful 2D information has been exhausted. Body orientation, ball control, contact mechanics, individual ability, annotation error and intrinsic outcome variation can contribute. Collective defensive behaviour and richer tactical context remain extensions. Tracking velocities use a centred seven-frame window: this offline benchmark is not a strictly causal live system.

A more flexible tree model with contextual features, the physics likelihood as an input and training-only resampling is a separate future architecture. The resampling experiments on the present likelihood did not show a convincing held-out benefit. Published numbers above are contextual benchmarks with their definitions and sampling differences recorded, not a same-dataset ranking.

## Pass-risk benchmark {#pass-risk-benchmark}

The selected pass model estimates **team completion probability** from the release state and a candidate destination. Parameters are fitted along reconstructed physical trajectories and transferred to a hypothetical potential pitch control field; its final calibration is isotonic. The [pass vignette](vignettes/02_pass_probability/02_pass_probability.ipynb) derives the equations and executes trajectory and pitch-field examples. The control/flight lineage is Spearman 2017 and *Beyond Expected Goals* [@spearman2017; @spearman2018beyond].

### Accepted cohort and endpoint checks

The benchmark contains **6,706 passes: 5,742 completions and 964 failures (14.38%), across ten SkillCorner matches**. Passers are outfield players; goalkeepers remain in the state and can receive or intercept passes. Duration from release to matched reception/recovery is in the inclusive interval **[0.5, 10] s**, matching the temporal selection in Spearman 2017, §3.1. All valid curvature levels are retained; Spearman additionally filtered curvature below 5%, so the cohorts differ. [@spearman2017]

Release and the immediate next individual-possession start must be matched in the same match/period, with positive chronology, no intervening annotated interruption and complete observed ball XY. For completed passes, the identified recipient must be the next carrier with a matched pass reception; for failures, the next endpoint is an opponent interception/recovery. The recovery location is a proxy for a failed pass's intended destination. Native-coordinate conversion, endpoint identity, tracking state and the five initial observations are checked. The passer's possession start and receiver's possession end need not both be matched.

From the former 7,078-pass cohort, 267 unsupported links were excluded: 69 annotated interruptions, three additional incomplete observed flights, 190 completions without an identifiable direct reception in the next possession, and five failed-pass links attributed to the same team. The 190 exclusions establish missing/unsupported receipt links under this rule, not 190 proven wrong success labels. The duration rule excludes another 104 short passes and one 11.1 s pass. Outcomes are not relabelled and later possessions are not substituted to rescue a link. These criteria are fixed independently of model residuals.

### Physics settings and initial conditions

The shared reachability settings are **v_max=5.5 m/s and a=a_turn=7 m/s²**. The speed cap is motivated by the off-ball upper tail after removing speed ≤2 m/s: the current pooled player-frame 95th percentile is 5.745 m/s, or 5.656 m/s using only frames without an annotated carrier as in the historical exploration. Thus 5.5 is a nearby empirical threshold tested against 5.0, not an exact empirical percentile. [Definitions and per-match quantiles](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/offball_speed_by_match.csv). Acceleration 7 and the reference speed 5 follow Spearman 2018; a universal cap represents average ability. [@spearman2018beyond]

The final TTI preserves the observed initial speed when it exceeds v_max: movement then uses that speed without additional acceleration. This **same TTI and settings are used along reconstructed paths for fitting, at candidate PPCF destinations, and for receiver arrival when selecting hypothetical flight time**. Below v_max, acceleration and cruise are unchanged. This is the only physical change from run22; trajectory construction, flight library, likelihood and integration remain fixed.

Initial position is observed at release. Two initial-condition estimators use five observations at 0..0.4 s: mean measured velocity and a fit to observed ball positions. The position fit estimates launch speed and direction, fixes release position, and has explicit fallback if numerical fitting fails. Boundary selection uses paired free-flight forecast error after 0.6 s and before the next control, averaged equally across fitting matches. It is repeated inside every fit set. **All outer folds and the final refit selected the position fit.** Centred ball-velocity smoothing extends the mean method's support through 0.6 s; this remains an offline study.

Reconstructed trajectories use gravity and constant drag (ρ=1.22, C_D=0.25, A=0.038, m=0.42, g=9.81 in SI units), without spin/Magnus. They are sampled to 10 s every 0.04 s. The historical path likelihood assigns an interval to every sample, giving 251 left steps or 10.04 s. Hypothetical PPCF uses exact target distances, a 30×30 launch grid over 5–25 m/s and 0–45°, and matches flight time to the teammate initially nearest the target, following Spearman's receiver-friendly timing construction. Target control is integrated for 15 s with 0.01 s exponential-Euler steps; the carrier is excluded before competing for mass. These numerical conventions are identical across the candidate arms. [@spearman2017; @spearman2018beyond]

### Estimation, calibration and held-out evaluation

λ_control and arrival dispersion s are estimated by **MLE on the natural Bernoulli trajectory likelihood**, without priors or a λ=30 cap. Positive parameters use log coordinates, BFGS with automatic gradients and line search starts from (λ,s)=(4.3,0.43),(3,0.3),(5,0.5), and fitting accumulates both outcomes in log space without a probability floor or parameter-dependent stopping rule. The hypothetical target PPCF is a distinct prediction problem; its transferred raw scores require calibration.

Five outer folds hold out two entire matches each. Within the remaining eight, four 6-fit/2-held-out rotations generate raw PPCF scores. An isotonic map is fitted to those internally held-out scores; physical parameters are then refitted on eight matches and evaluated, with that fixed map, on the two outer test matches. Boundary selection and parameter fitting never use those test matches. Platt uses the same calibration examples. The final run fixes v_max=5.5 and uses exactly the run22 match partitions and test examples. Its comparison with run22 is paired; the earlier v_max=5.0 sensitivity remains archived. No resampling is used.

The final operational fit uses all ten matches; its isotonic map is fitted to outer cross-fitted raw PPCF scores. It is separate from the nested OOF evaluation. ECE uses ten equal-count quantile bins; gain is 1−CE/CE_null, with each null estimated from its outer training matches. Reported CE uses natural logarithms and metric clipping at 1e-6. The ten matches also informed model and calibration choices, so this is a **development benchmark**, without an untouched external test.

### Results

| Model / calibration | TTI | CE ↓ | Gain over null ↑ | ECE q10 ↓ |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Trajectory MLE + isotonic, historical run22 | Cruise at cap | 0.141912 | 65.57% | 0.353% |
| Fixed λ=4.3,s=0.43 + isotonic | Preserve initial overspeed | 0.140562 | 65.90% | 0.289% |
| Trajectory MLE, raw | Preserve initial overspeed | 0.150555 | 63.48% | 4.040% |
| Trajectory MLE + Platt | Preserve initial overspeed | 0.130010 | 68.46% | 0.814% |
| **Trajectory MLE + isotonic — final run41** | **Preserve initial overspeed** | **0.131121** | **68.19%** | **0.183%** |

The training-fold null CE is 0.412222. The final isotonic model reduces CE by 0.010791 against run22, or **2.618 percentage points of gain over the null**. CE improves in eight of ten matches after isotonic and in all ten before calibration. Isotonic remains selected for calibrated probabilities; Platt has slightly lower CE. The fixed-coefficient row retains the historical code's s=0.43, rather than claiming it is Spearman's fitted s. [Current metrics](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/metrics.csv), [paired comparisons](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/paired_comparisons.csv), [archived run22](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/old/run22_pre_uniform_tti_20261022/metrics.csv).

![Held-out calibration and curvature diagnostic](figures/pass_benchmark_calibration.png)

All 25 inner/outer MLE fits passed the gradient checks. All 75 optimizer starts reached the same NLL within 7.28×10⁻¹²; the maximum selected absolute gradient was 2.80×10⁻⁵ and no weak identification was flagged. Outer-fold estimates are λ_control=5.164–5.930 s⁻¹ and s=0.2842–0.3004 s. The corresponding run22 ranges were 4.942–5.540 and 0.3223–0.3400. These are fold-specific estimates, not the deployed weights.

The **installed full-data model** refits the same trajectory likelihood on all ten matches, using the run41 TTI and a final isotonic map fitted to its outer cross-fitted raw PPCF scores. It has **λ_control=5.437830 s⁻¹ and s=0.294560 s**. It is not an additional test fold or an average of fold parameters. The public reader reproduces all 6,706 raw scores within 1.02e-08; field probes include initial overspeed cases. [Refit provenance](docs/pass-risk-refit-provenance.json), [benchmark provenance](docs/pass-risk-benchmark-provenance.json), [frozen specification](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/frozen_specification.json).

For context, Spearman 2017 §4 reports λ=4.30 s⁻¹ and temporal dispersion σ=0.45 s, whereas the historical code used s=0.43. Our λ remains of the same order and s is smaller. These effective parameters depend on tracking, movement/flight approximations and the fitting cohort; the comparison does not establish numerical equality or physiological constants. [@spearman2017]

### Comparison with published work

| Study / selected model | CE | Gain over null | ECE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| PRESS trajectory MLE + isotonic, final uniform TTI | 0.131121 | 68.19% | 0.183% |
| Fernández et al. 2021, SoccerMap pass success | 0.1900 | ≈62.40%* | 0.470% |
| Stalpaert 2022, CatBoost comprehensive + formation | 0.2087 | 63.85% | 0.310% |

These results are **in line with the available academic benchmarks** in relative loss reduction and calibration; the lower PRESS CE is not evidence of superiority across datasets. Prevalence, league, sample size, endpoint selection, features and validation protocols differ. Fernández reports validation temperature calibration for pass success; Stalpaert tests isotonic but does not retain it for the final pass-risk component. [@fernandez2021; @stalpaert2022]

*Fernández does not provide the corresponding test-fold null in this table. The approximate gain uses entropy of the reported overall completion share79.64%, giving CE_null≈0.505353; it is contextual and not an exact recovered test-null comparison. Stalpaert's gain uses its reported null0.5773. [Source locators and assumptions](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/literature_comparison.csv).

### Curvature and the flight-model limitation

Curvature is the maximum perpendicular XY deviation from the release-to-target line divided by endpoint distance, expressed as a percentage. It is computed retrospectively and is used only for this diagnostic. **Both groups use the same all-pass-trained model and calibrator**, without curvature-specific refitting.

| Held-out subset | Passes | Failure share | CE | Gain over subgroup null | ECE q10 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All accepted passes | 6,706 | 14.38% | 0.131121 | 68.19% | 0.183% |
| Curvature <10% | 5,211 | 12.36% | 0.097953 | 73.84% | 0.227% |
| Curvature ≥10% | 1,495 | 21.40% | 0.246731 | 52.65% | 1.170% |

Subgroup nulls are estimated within the corresponding outer training subgroup. Quantile bins use stable score sorting after canonical match/pass/frame ordering, including tied isotonic plateaus. Gains against the all-pass training null are exported separately; they are not the subgroup-null gains in this table. [Curvature metrics](data/benchmarks/pass_risk/curvature_metrics.csv).

The degradation on non-straight passes is consistent with **remaining headroom in the simplified flight model and its initial-condition estimation**. Missing spin/Magnus is a plausible contributor, because this model cannot generate lateral curvature. It is not isolated causally by this comparison: curved passes also differ in geometry, difficulty, prevalence and tracking quality. Better supported flight/boundary models are a natural extension; the accepted benchmark retains all valid curved passes rather than selecting an easier training population.

Other limitations are destination-based interception as a proxy for early blocks, average player capabilities, uncertain intended destinations for failures, endpoint annotation noise, ten-match development data and centred smoothing. Shorter passes need a boundary estimator restricted to their observed free-flight support; they remain outside this accepted cohort. The archived historical curvature split and earlier runs remain available under `data/benchmarks/pass_risk/old/`, separate from these final results.

## Pass selection: planned fixed-configuration comparison

**Protocol specification; the new comparison has not yet produced benchmark results.**
The experiment compares a shared XGBoost destination utility with and without
teammate cross-nesting. It uses 6,810 choices from ten matches, with six fit,
two validation and two test matches per outer fold. There are 19 original
variables, represented by 48 columns after one-hot encoding start type and
previous action. Candidate-cell rows within a choice are dependent; the large
matrix does not constitute millions of independent decisions.

Before freezing the final configuration, a single-split capacity pilot is
planned with the following four settings, each fitted both flat and with
cross-nesting: depth6/child5, depth3/child5, depth4/child20 and depth4/child1.
Learning rate remains 0.05, L2 remains 1 and all other settings are unchanged.
The depth3 versus depth6 pair probes whether more complex interactions can
extract additional signal from the same features at the same child threshold;
the two depth4 fits vary the minimum curvature support at fixed interaction
depth. Every fit uses validation early stopping rather than screening at an
early tree count. The pilot never scores the two test matches. Its validation
ranking is descriptive and does not automatically select a final model for
small gains. Similar results would establish limited sensitivity to these
four probes, not separate the effects of data scale and feature information.

If the curves motivate it, a subsequent L2=3 or 10 probe may be considered
only for depth6/child5 and depth4/child1; it is not in the eight current fits.
A low best iteration alone is not evidence of overfitting. Small differences
lead to retaining the depth4/child5 reference below and moving to the separate
v>vmax check. Since that reference is not among the four pilot settings,
a subsequent five-fold comparison at the reference configuration would need
ten additional fits; choosing one of the pilot settings would allow reusing
its two selected checkpoints and require eight additional fits. Global pilot
selection would make the subsequent five-fold evaluation exploratory rather
than independently nested hyperparameter selection.

The reference configuration below is specified to compare model structures
within a bounded compute budget. The following rationales are project design choices, informed
by the [XGBoost tuning guidance](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/release_3.2.0/tutorials/param_tuning.html),
not claims that the exact values are universally recommended or optimal.

| Setting | Value | Rationale for this comparison |
|---|---|---|
| `max_depth` | 4 | At most 16 leaves per tree: allow geometry/context interactions while containing fragmentation of a few thousand fit choices. Feature count alone does not determine depth. |
| `eta` | 0.05 | Apply small utility corrections while the nested model also updates its scale. Smaller steps would require more tree updates; this is an explicit speed/update-size compromise. |
| `reg_lambda` | 1 | Quadratic leaf regularization with the unit default scale, without imposing a large additional penalty that has not been calibrated. |
| `min_child_weight` | 5 | Require positive aggregate curvature support for child nodes, with a stricter threshold than the default 1. This discourages weakly supported partitions; the threshold is a conservative design choice, not five observations or an estimated optimum. |
| `subsample` | 0.8 | Moderate randomization of per-tree contributions, retaining their majority to avoid aggressive data reduction. |
| `colsample_bytree` | 0.8 | Vary the available predictors across trees when spatial and contextual predictors are correlated, while retaining most encoded columns. |
| `gamma` / `reg_alpha` | 0 / 0 | Avoid introducing an additional split-gain threshold or L1 leaf sparsity on top of depth, L2 and curvature constraints. |
| `tree_method` / `max_bin` | `hist` / 256 | Bound split-search cost on the large candidate matrix using native histogram training and its default resolution. |
| Maximum trees | 2,000 | Explicit compute ceiling that allows gradual learning; reaching it is reported as budget exhaustion, not convergence. |
| Early stopping | 100 rounds | Select the minimum validation choice NLL with patience for gradual improvement; the RUMBoost case study uses this patience. |
| Initial utilities / nesting | 0 / ρ=1 | Uniform destination probabilities and the flat-limit nesting initialization, without imposing an initial destination preference or within-nest correlation. |
| Randomness | One fixed seed per fold, common across families; `seed_per_iteration=True` | Reproducible stochastic policy without seed selection. This policy is not claimed to improve accuracy; run30 used a different RNG policy. |

Parameter definitions and software defaults are documented by
[XGBoost](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/release_3.2.0/parameter.html).
The regularized leaf update is $w^*=-G/(H+\lambda)$, before learning-rate
shrinkage, with $G$ and $H$ the gradient and curvature sums supplied to the
booster ([Chen and Guestrin, §2.2](https://arxiv.org/html/1603.02754v3)).
Consequently L2 and the minimum child threshold depend on the numerical scale
of the supplied curvature. Matching their values is a matched training recipe,
not proof of identical effective regularization between MNL and CNL.
Subsampling occurs in native tree construction after derivatives have been
computed using every candidate in each choice; the categorical denominator
is not approximated by a sampled choice set.

The derivative and curvature rules follow the archived CPU RUMBoost source,
including its CNL second-order approximation rather than an asserted exact
Hessian diagonal. Its additive case study uses depth 1 to disallow interactions;
that constraint is not transferred to this interaction-capable task.
[RUMBoost manuscript, §§3.1–3.2](https://arxiv.org/html/2401.11954v1).

For nesting, the shared parameter is optimized by fit-only SLSQP every 20
tree updates, initialized at its current value, with relaxation 0.1 in
ρ=1/μ. The interval and relaxation reproduce the current
[RUMBoost implementation](https://github.com/big-ucl/rumboost/blob/main/rumboost/rumboost.py),
which is distinct from the parameter-search protocol in its early manuscript.
One common parameter avoids assigning a persistent meaning to changing
teammate slots. Fixed memberships from individual raw pitch control connect
destinations to potential receivers without observing the future receiver.
The project uses ρ∈[1,10] (μ∈[0.1,1]), a numerical bound permitting stronger
nesting than the upstream default [1,2.5]; boundary fits will be identified.
Failed, nonfinite or uphill relaxed scale updates are rejected. These are
explicit task adaptations, not a full replication of RUMBoost's LightGBM
architecture. A single conditional start limits cost without a claim of
global joint optimality.

Ten fits are planned. Validation selects the joint tree-prefix/scale
checkpoint before test evaluation. Fit NLL is logged every 50 trees alongside
per-tree validation NLL to diagnose learning behavior. These matches have
already informed model development, so results will remain exploratory.
